item.title: How the Postal Service Became Central to U.S. Elections
item.description:
Days before the election of 1864, Pvt. Isaac Walters watched a group of soldiers leave a Union hospital in Virginia. They had been granted furloughs to travel hundreds of miles home to vote.

Walters wished he could join them. “They will all get to vote for President I Suppose,” he wrote his sister-in-law, in a letter preserved at the National Postal Museum in Washington, D.C.

More than 160 years later, voting from afar is again at the center of a fight over American democracy. The Supreme Court on Monday blocked the Trump administration’s plan to use the Postal Service to screen mail ballots, the latest chapter in the long and sometimes contentious relationship between the nation’s postal system and its elections.

The postal system was created in part to bring together and inform citizens of a sprawling republic. It later helped Americans away from home cast their ballots, weathered a transformation in its funding and a collapse in traditional mail, and became a political flashpoint when voting by mail peaked during the coronavirus pandemic.

Before the American Revolution, colonists built an alternative to the British mail system that connected groups and allowed them to communicate beyond the reach of Crown postmasters, according to the National Postal Museum. In 1775, the Continental Congress adopted the idea and named Benjamin Franklin the first postmaster general.

The Post Office Act of 1792 reflected the founders’ belief that the mail system could help sustain the new republic. George Washington championed a broad postal network to spread knowledge of the government’s laws and proceedings. James Madison warned against high postage rates that would inhibit the “distribution of knowledge and information throughout the Union.”

Congress made newspapers especially cheap to mail, helping to support an informed electorate. The law also protected the privacy of correspondence and gave Congress control over new postal routes.

Postal Service records show that the network grew with the country, from 75 post offices in 1790 to more than 28,000 by 1860. The idea of using it to facilitate voting away from home was emerging: Pennsylvania allowed soldiers to cast absentee ballots from the field during the War of 1812, and New Jersey passed similar legislation in 1815.

Absentee voting was not entirely new, but it became widespread during the Civil War and turned into a partisan issue.

As President Abraham Lincoln sought re-election in 1864, hundreds of thousands of voters were on battlefields far from home. Nineteen Union states allowed troops to vote away from their usual polling places via field polling places, proxies and mail, according to the Library of Congress.

The changes prompted accusations of fraud and intimidation, including absentee ballot-stuffing and Lincoln administration officials pressuring soldiers, according to Jonathan W. White, a Civil War historian.

The balloting processes varied. In Ohio, soldiers voted in camps and hospitals, and election officials mailed the tallies home in specially printed envelopes. Other states used the mail to carry ballots or proxy votes.

The Civil War established an enduring precedent: Americans unable to reach the polls did not have to forfeit their votes. Absentee voting gradually expanded beyond the military, and later wars also prompted the government to find ways to accommodate millions of Americans far from home.

After a major strike by federal postal workers in 1970, Congress replaced the cabinet-level Post Office Department with the largely self-financing United States Postal Service.

Decades later, the internet eroded its traditional business. Postal Service data show that total mail volume peaked at 213 billion pieces in 2006, and the Government Accountability Office found that it fell by about 20 percent in just four years. By 2020, first-class mail volume was roughly half its peak from two decades earlier.

During the coronavirus pandemic, states passed new laws making it easier to vote by mail for the 2020 election to protect public health. Nearly 70 million Americans turned to mail ballots for the 2020 election, according to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission, even as the newly appointed postmaster general, Louis DeJoy, imposed operational changes and cost-cutting measures that slowed some mail delivery.

At the same time, President Trump amplified unfounded claims of widespread fraud in mail voting, while Democrats accused his administration of trying to suppress votes. The Postal Service became a focus of congressional hearings, lawsuits and the broader fight over voting.

Mr. Trump returned to office last year still falsely claiming that the 2020 election that he lost had been rigged. He continued to attack mail voting, calling it “mail-in-cheating,” despite casting his own ballot by mail in a special election in Florida in March 2026. It was not the first time he had voted by mail.

Later that month, Mr. Trump signed an executive order giving the Postal Service new authority to screen mail ballots by requiring states to share lists of voters ahead of time. Election officials warned that the system could disenfranchise voters and cause chaos.

On Monday, the Supreme Court blocked the administration’s ballot-screening plan, which had been challenged by two dozen states and multiple voting rights groups.

item.title: Steve Bannon and Bernie Sanders Condemn Tech ‘Oligarchs’ and Demand A.I. Reforms
item.description:
In thundering, back-to-back speeches, Senator Bernie Sanders and Stephen K. Bannon on Tuesday denounced the billionaires who run the country’s largest tech companies and urged Americans to demand tighter restrictions on artificial intelligence before its capabilities exceed human control.

The unusual public appearances by the country’s elder democratic socialist and a leading architect of the MAGA movement, at a conference in Washington, underscored the deep and rising anxiety over the potential destructive power of artificial intelligence. As calls to regulate the technology have grown louder, transcending political allegiances, there is little consensus from Congress or the White House about what a national policy would look like.

“When you are racing towards a cliff,” Mr. Sanders said, “you hit the brakes.” He added, “We are at a dangerous and unprecedented moment in world history. And it is imperative for all of us to stand up.”

Everyone attending the event, the Pro-Human Assembly, seemed in agreement about the threat that A.I. may someday wipe out humanity. But for a few hours, A.I. produced a less catastrophic outcome: It united the participants — Republican and Democratic politicians, evangelical Christian, Mormon and Catholic leaders, artists and others — in agreement that human beings, not machines, should control their own destinies.

The conference, which was hosted by the nonprofit Future of Life Institute, drew several hundred people who listened to hours of speeches about the deepening anxiety in Silicon Valley, Washington and beyond about the race to rein in A.I. before its computing power becomes unstoppable.

A slogan embroidered on hats being handed out to attendees captured the sentiment shared by most carbon-based life-forms in the room: “Keep the future human.”

Such concerns have intensified with surprising speed lately.

Last week, an Anthropic researcher who had previously worked at OpenAI went public with his decision to resign, saying that he believed both companies were acting irresponsibly.

In response, the chief executives of the A.I. start-ups Anthropic and OpenAI acknowledged their own fears that their technologies are advancing at an alarming pace.

Seven in 10 Americans said they are afraid A.I. will weaken human bonds, according to a poll released this week by Elon University, and about six in 10 say A.I.’s potential to take over most human tasks will undermine an individual’s sense of purpose. A separate poll from The New York Times found that 61 percent of likely voters oppose the construction of data centers, the massive warehouses that power A.I.

But there is little agreement in Washington about how to mandate a slower, more regulated approach to A.I. development. The White House and congressional leaders have sent conflicting signals. On Monday, President Trump dismissed calls for safety guardrails on A.I., calling fears of the technology as a “hoax.” He warned he could take criminal action against the heads of A.I. companies for any harms created by their technologies.

Anthropic declined to comment and OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and its partner, Microsoft, accusing them of copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. OpenAI and Microsoft have denied those claims.)

At the conference, speakers pitched a wide array of regulatory proposals, without consensus on whether regulators should intervene to fully stop the development of A.I. Some leaders conceded they struggled to understand the technology.

Representative Greg Casar, for instance, proposed one solution the tech industry has resisted. “The answer is simple: We ban A.I. systems that are too powerful for humans to control,” said Mr. Casar, Democrat of Texas.

The speeches on Tuesday also conveyed, with a sense of disbelief from the speakers, about how such obvious, uncontroversial statements about human dignity needed to be said out loud.

“I can’t believe I have to say this,” said Representative Lori Trahan, Democrat of Massachusetts. “The future we all want is human. It’s nonnegotiable.”

“If we lose grip on this technology, we don’t lose grip as Republicans or Democrats,” Ms. Trahan continued, as she was interrupted by applause. “We lose it as human beings.”

A Catholic archbishop, an evangelical pastor and an elder from the Mormon Church voiced a wide variety of concerns.

Salvatore J. Cordileone, the archbishop of San Francisco, urged people to seize their agency while they still can. “We have to be the masters of A.I.,” he said.

His speech raised an unknown that weighed heavily on the minds of many at the conference: Is it already too late?

This heavy question and others were left largely unanswered.

Walter Kim, president of the National Association of Evangelicals, asked whether humans would be living without purpose in a world of “frictionless existence,” where he said A.I. is expected to solve most problems.

Ashley Judd, the actor and the chief negotiator for the union SAG-AFTRA, spoke for many in Hollywood about how A.I. has led to the spread of images of sexual abuse and disinformation.

Parents of teenagers who died by suicide after developing relationships with chatbots delivered tearful appeals for child safety regulation.

Representative Chip Roy, Republican of Texas, recalled encounters with constituents who described feeling powerless as data centers went up in their communities, with little consultation, and as their children became obsessed with technology they didn’t understand.

Technology, he said, should be a tool that people consciously decide to use, not the other way around. “We are not supposed to be tools for data collection and technology,” he said.

Both Mr. Sanders and Mr. Bannon decried the absence of any meaningful input into A.I. regulation by the tens of millions of working Americans whose lives they said would be most upended by A.I.

Mr. Sanders has introduced legislation to pause development of data centers and called for Mr. Trump to form an accord with the president of China, Xi Jinping, to ban superintelligent A.I.

Mr. Bannon said he doesn’t believe legislation will slow down A.I. because of Congress’ inaction. Instead, he called for presidential executive order to slow down development and ensure the biggest tech firms aren’t able to extend their power through their grip on the A.I. industry.

“American citizens are not going to be supplicants to the oligarchs anymore,” declared Mr. Bannon, who noted that despite the obvious areas of disagreement between him and Mr. Sanders, the high stakes of the moment demanded partisanship be set aside.

“We have to rise above it,” Mr. Bannon said. “This is a hinge in history.”

item.title: Court Tosses Immigrant’s Conviction Over Agents’ Secret Facebook Group
item.description:
An appeals court on Monday overturned a Mexican man’s criminal conviction for illegally entering the United States, ruling that prosecutors withheld evidence that Border Patrol agents were members of a secret Facebook group that posted racist content.

A three-judge panel for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit found that the government violated its constitutional obligation to disclose relevant evidence when it failed to share that two of the three Border Patrol agents testifying against the immigrant, Jaime Tovar-Duran, had been part of a private Facebook group called “I’m 10-15.”

The group, named for a law enforcement code for undocumented immigrants in custody, became notorious for its racist and otherwise offensive posts after it was uncovered in July 2019 by the investigative news site ProPublica and prompted a congressional investigation.

On Monday, the appeals court ordered a lower court to determine whether the agents’ membership in the Facebook group would have affected the guilty verdict in Mr. Tovar-Duran’s case, who according to court documents, was apprehended in November 2019 after crossing into the United States from Mexico a few days after he had been deported.

“In light of the derogatory material posted in the group, the witnesses’ activity on the page could be strong evidence of bias against noncitizens,” Circuit Judge Ana de Alba wrote.

In July 2019, an internal investigation by Customs and Border Protection identified 70 former and then-current C.P.B. employees as members of Facebook groups and other social media pages that included obscene images of Hispanic lawmakers and threats to members of Congress.

The “I’m 10-15” group included posts questioning whether a photograph of a dead migrant father and child was staged, and it depicted doctored, sexually explicit photos of Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York. C.B.P. officials said discriminatory and harassing posts had violated standards of conduct but that membership in a group alone would not automatically compel punishment.

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment on Tuesday about whether the agents involved in Mr. Tovar-Duran’s case were members of the Facebook group and had faced any disciplinary action. C.B.P. did not answer questions about the case.

According to court documents, a Border Patrol agent encountered Mr. Tovar-Duran about three miles from the Tecate, Calif., port of entry. The agent testified that Mr. Tovar-Duran told him he was from Mexico and did not have immigration documents that would allow him to remain in the United States legally.

Initially, prosecutors said none of the agents involved in the case had been members of the Facebook group. But shortly before trial, they told the defense lawyers that two of their three witnesses, including one agent who said he had interviewed Mr. Tovar-Duran and another who said he reviewed his immigration records, were part of the Facebook group. Prosecutors said the witnesses did not recall posting or liking any content in the group.

In 2020, Mr. Tovar-Duran was convicted of improper entry, a misdemeanor, and sentenced to time served by a magistrate judge. He was subsequently deported to Mexico. Mr. Tovar-Duran appealed his conviction to the district court, arguing that the judge had erred by denying his repeated requests to require the prosecution to provide information about the Border Patrol agents’ membership in the Facebook group.

The district judge said that even if the agents were in the Facebook group, there was enough evidence to convict Mr. Tovar-Duran of illegal entry.

The appeals court disagreed in its ruling on Monday, saying that they “could not determine” whether the government’s failure to disclose their group membership had “prejudiced” the defendant.

Kim Hutchison, a lawyer for Mr. Tovar-Duran, said the ruling showed why due process was necessary.

The government “tried to use these shortcuts like not offering full discovery,” and that’s why the conviction was reversed, Ms. Hutchison said. She added that because her client was now living in Mexico, it was not clear how the case would proceed, since Mr. Tovar-Duran may not be able to appear in person for a hearing, as is usually required.

The U.S. attorney’s office for the Southern District of California, which prosecuted the case, did not immediately return a request for comment.

According to a House Oversight and Reform Committee report, C.B.P. officials were aware of misconduct in the “I’m 10-15” group since August 2016 but took minimal action until media began reporting on it three years later.

Investigations into the misconduct resulted in discipline for a small number of agents, the congressional report found. Although a disciplinary board recommended two dozen firings, only two people lost their jobs.

item.title: Federal Employees Were Paid $9.5 Billion Not to Work in 2025 Under DOGE Effort
item.description:
The Trump administration paid federal employees $9.5 billion not to work during 2025, part of the president’s plan to reduce the size of the federal bureaucracy and government spending, according to a new estimate from a congressional watchdog.

The Department of Government Efficiency’s program to shrink the federal work force through deferred resignations increased the use of paid administrative leave by 435 percent during the first year of President Trump’s second term, the Government Accountability Office said in a report on Tuesday. That represents a sixfold increase since 2023.

Drastically reducing the size of the federal work force was part of a broader Trump administration plan to rein in what it called frivolous and wasteful federal spending, with an initial promise of $1 trillion in savings.

The administration has said its efforts have led to more than $200 billion in savings, a figure that outside experts have not independently confirmed. In addition, the federal deficit has increased since Mr. Trump returned to office, in part because of the war in Iran and the sweeping tax cuts that Republicans enacted in 2025.

During a congressional hearing on Tuesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a government initiative to cut spending “is coming.”

Spending on civilian salaries and benefits represents a small fraction of the total federal budget. Yet it was among the Trump administration’s first targets for cutting costs.

In a January 2025 email, the Trump administration offered a proposition to about two million federal workers with the subject line “Fork in the Road.” It was billed as a one-time-only offer to pay workers through September 2025 if they resigned within the next nine days. The offer came with the warning to the employees that they were likely to be fired eventually as the Trump administration sought to decrease the size of the federal government.

The federal civilian work force has shrunk by about 12 percent since Mr. Trump returned to office, according to data from the Office of Personnel Management, as a result of resignations, firings and new hires. But the agency has not been able to identify the long- term savings, the accountability office found.

The Office of Personnel Management did not respond to a request for comment.

Of the $9.5 billion in paid administrative leave, the congressional watchdog said that about $6.7 billion was associated with the deferred resignation program, which agencies continued to offer at other points during 2025. According to federal data, 139,963 federal employees took the deferred resignation offer.

The largest number of deferred resignations were among civilian employees at the Agriculture, Defense and Treasury Departments.

Critics have faulted the Trump administration for losing generations of expertise in the purge at the expense of Americans who have relied on federal programs.

“Trump spent billions to push out experienced and badly needed experts across government — this was the most expensive way imaginable to make government worse,” Senator Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, said in a statement on Tuesday.

Hasty efforts to achieve Mr. Trump’s downsizing mandates led some agencies to rescind deferred resignation offers or hire people to replace employees who left. The Partnership for Public Service, which advocates a more effective federal work force, found that the federal government has backfilled more than 20,000 positions left vacant because of deferred resignations.

Since the downsizing, the federal government has initiated recruiting efforts to hire employees, including lawyers and tech workers, after so many departures in 2025. There has also been an emphasis in hiring more early-career employees.

“What I really want to see is more people like Big Balls,” Scott Kupor, the director of the personnel office, said on Monday in an interview with right-wing podcaster Benny Johnson. Mr. Kupor was using the online pseudonym for Edward Coristine, the DOGE employee who was hired at 19 last year to slash the federal bureaucracy.

“We need people who are patriotic, who say: ‘You know what? I care about this country. I’m willing to do something good,’” Mr. Kupor said, making the case that young hires like Mr. Coristine can work in the federal government for a couple of years and not an entire career. Mr. Coristine now works in a new White House office focused on improving the design of government websites.

Nicholas Nehamas contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Approves $2.8 Billion Arms Sale to Israel, Including 40,000 One-Ton Bombs
item.description:
The Trump administration has approved a $2.8 billion sale of heavy bombs to Israel, according to a U.S. official, in what would be among the largest deliveries of U.S. munitions there even as American public support for the country declines.

The proposed sale would include 40,000 one-ton bombs whose use by Israel in Gaza and Lebanon has drawn international anger because of the civilian harm caused by their wide blast radius.

Human rights groups and some foreign governments have condemned Israel for dropping the giant munitions in densely populated areas, sometimes killing dozens of civilians in strikes targeting just one individual.

The package would include 20,000 each of America’s 2,000-pound MK-84 and BLU-117 bombs. It would also provide Israel with 20,000 bunker-busting I-2000 penetrator warheads, which explode on delay after smashing through an outer surface like soil, rock or concrete. The plan was reported earlier by The Washington Post.

The blast from a 2,000-pound bomb can be lethal at more than 1,000 feet and leave a crater as deep as 50 feet. Israel provoked a fierce outcry after it dropped hundreds of the heavy bombs on Gaza.

The State Department recently sent the proposed deal to two congressional committees to get informal approval, the U.S. official said.

Production and delivery of the munitions usually takes months or years, but there are ways to expedite the process.

In mid-2024, the Biden administration paused a shipment of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel because of concern about their use in crowded civilian areas. President Trump allowed the shipment to proceed days after taking office last January.

Then in February, the Trump administration agreed to sell roughly $2.7 billion in munitions to Israel, a package that included 35,000 of the one-ton MK-84 and BLU-117 bombs.

While congressional leaders can tell the Trump administration that they oppose the deal, Secretary of State Marco Rubio can exercise emergency powers to proceed with the sale regardless, as he has done repeatedly, or just say he is moving forward with it. The administration would then bypass getting informal approval from Congress and formally announce the sale is happening.

In those cases, both the House and Senate would need to pass a resolution to block the deal. Such a resolution would require the support of two-thirds of each body to guarantee it can overcome a presidential veto.

The Biden administration also declared an emergency in the region to bypass congressional approval and expedite shipments of arms to Israel twice during the Israel-Gaza war. One of those packages included 13,000 rounds of tank ammunition, and the second included artillery munitions.

The State Department’s approval of such a large package of devastating munitions reflects Mr. Trump’s continued strong support for Israel despite his recent disputes with its prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, over the country’s military operations in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Mr. Netanyahu is expected to be in New York next week to address the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly.

The State Department said in a statement that as a matter of policy it would not confirm or comment on a proposed arms sale that has not been formally notified to Congress.

The proposed deal is sure to draw strong opposition among Democrats in Congress, some of whom have called for ending all U.S. aid to Israel in response to the huge civilian toll of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel.

But anger toward Israel has also risen among Mr. Trump’s traditional supporters. The former Fox News host Tucker Carlson posted a tirade on social media that excoriated Israel for what he called the “slaughter” of Palestinians in Gaza.

Mr. Carlson also said that the added destructive power would embolden Israel and fuel the conflict with Iran launched jointly by the U.S. and Israel in February. Mr. Carlson has adamantly opposed the offensive and blames Mr. Netanyahu for convincing Mr. Trump to approve it. “If you wanted to extend the Iran war into the indefinite future, this is exactly what you’d do,” Mr. Carlson wrote.

Israel argues that Hamas fighters in Gaza and Hezbollah militants in Lebanon intentionally embed themselves among civilians — sometimes in bunkers or tunnels that require heavy munitions to penetrate — to force Israel to kill innocent civilians and face international pressure.

But many former U.S. officials and military analysts question whether Israel has been too quick to pass up less destructive alternatives. The U.S. provides Israel a base line of $3.8 billion a year in military assistance, including $3.3 billion in financing that Israel largely uses to purchase American weapons, which includes the latest sale of bombs.Another $500 million in U.S. aid is earmarked annually for joint missile-defense programs. Mr. Trump has repeatedly butted heads with Mr. Netanyahu over Israel’s military operations outside its borders, which have on several occasions complicated U.S. efforts to negotiate lasting peace in Gaza and to resolve the conflict with Iran — to Mr. Trump’s great frustration.But Mr. Trump has expressed far less public concern about civilian casualties than did Mr. Biden, who also was sharply criticized for being too tolerant of such deaths.

item.title: Event at Berkeley Mocking Charlie Kirk Draws Federal Criticism
item.description:
Emily Salib, a freshman at the University of California, Berkeley, stopped last Thursday evening at one of the campus’s main lawns to see what had drawn so many people to the area.

She paused to watch when she realized it was a so-called Kirkversary event. The gathering, pegged to the anniversary of Charlie Kirk’s murder, had been inspired by countless internet memes that have circulated online since Mr. Kirk’s death on Sept. 10, 2025.

The event at Berkeley has since drawn the attention of a top State Department official, who warned that international students were putting their visas at risk by celebrating the death of the conservative activist and co-founder of the political organization Turning Point USA.

It is unclear if any of the people who participated in the event, including those who opposed Mr. Kirk’s politics, were foreign students on visas.

Students sang and cheered at the event, according to the student newspaper, The Daily Californian. Someone brought a picture of the Mona Lisa with Mr. Kirk’s face on it. An advertising flyer promoted it as “an event to remember & gather.”

For people who don’t live online, it can be hard to appreciate the ubiquitous nature of memes about Mr. Kirk during the last 12 months. His face has been superimposed onto photos of athletes, politicians, entertainers and even great works of art. Some memes have lauded his legacy as a supporter of free speech. But many come out of left-leaning criticism of Mr. Kirk, who held strongly conservative views on guns, gender and race.

The event was an outgrowth of that online culture, said Ms. Salib, 18, from Virginia Beach, Va. She plans to study political science.

Mr. Kirk was shot to death last year while speaking at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah. Police have charged Tyler James Robinson, 23, of Washington, Utah, with Mr. Kirk’s murder. He has pleaded not guilty.

The controversy over such events as “Kirkversary” touches on the fraught debate about what speech goes too far on a college campus.

A photograph of a University of Utah student with a cake that said “Happy Kirkiversary” — one of several alternate spellings — triggered numerous accusations of harassment that has prompted the school to review the incident. And Carnegie Mellon University said this week that a professor had violated the university’s standards in a mocking social media post about the anniversary of Mr. Kirk’s murder.

On Saturday, Christopher Landau, the deputy secretary of state and one of the top officials at the department, replied to a post on X that purported to show students at the Berkeley event.

“Thanks,” Mr. Landau wrote. “On it!”

On Sunday, he posted on social media that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had “frequently underscored that a US visa is a privilege, not a right,” and that “foreigners who celebrate violence and political assassination aren’t welcome guests in our country.”

He linked to a statement from August that said the State Department under President Trump had revoked more than 175,000 visas, including from “multiple foreign nationals who celebrated the assassination of Charlie Kirk.”

The State Department press office responded to an interview request for Mr. Landau by referring to his social media posts on X.

Ms. Salib, the Berkeley student, said that although she did not like Mr. Kirk’s politics, she could understand why fans of Mr. Kirk would be put off by the campus event. She said she was horrified by his murder.

“The way our generation is handling the situation, with the light, laughing tone — I definitely see how that would be offensive to those who appreciated and supported Charlie Kirk,” she said.

But deportation threats? “That is pretty terrifying, actually,” Ms. Salib said. “Peaceful protest is at the core of American democracy.”

Earlier in the day, the campus’s chapter of Turning Point USA held an event commemorating Mr. Kirk’s life and death.

Janet Gilmore, a spokeswoman for the university, said in a statement that Berkeley “supports free speech on campus.” She said that the university was aware that a local chapter of Turning Point USA had gathered on campus to honor Mr. Kirk.

She said the university did not have details about the events and had not heard of any concerns that were reported to the police. “However we are looking into the matter,” she added.

Berkeley, a symbol of liberal politics long despised by many conservatives, has been a frequent target of Trump administration scrutiny.

Last fall, the Justice Department opened an investigation in the wake of protests during an event hosted by Turning Point USA. The department has not announced any findings in that inquiry, though it did accuse Berkeley’s law school last week of illegally discriminating against white and Asian applicants. The university has denied the allegations.

The Education Department and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission have also conducted investigations involving Berkeley. And researchers at Berkeley were among those who had their grant money cut. The Health and Human Services Department, for example, acknowledged in a July court filing that it had used Berkeley’s name to help identify research money to cut.

Alan Blinder contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Defended A.I. Data Centers on Truth Social, and Commenters Clapped Back
item.description:
President Trump posted on Truth Social this week that artificial intelligence and the data centers that power it “will be the Greatest Economic Development Engine in History ­­— Bigger than Oil, Gold, Diamonds, or even the Internet.”

Many of the commenters on his A.I. posts disagreed.

In hundreds of replies to Mr. Trump’s Truth Social posts this week, commenters criticized his enthusiasm, offering a social media snapshot that mirrors recent polling, which shows that Republicans are increasingly concerned about the technology. The New York Times analyzed thousands of comments on Mr. Trump’s posts to create a snapshot of what his most loyal supporters are thinking about his pro-A.I. stance.

Truth Social, which Mr. Trump created in 2022, has a user base that is relatively small compared with other social networks, with about 6 million users. But it remains a vital social space for Mr. Trump’s most ardent supporters, who typically create an enthusiastic echo chamber for the president’s ideas and rarely register opposition in big numbers.

Overall, the number of comments disparaging A.I. and data centers outnumbered those supporting the technology by nearly four to one, the analysis showed. Many of the comments criticizing the president came from users whose profiles suggested they were otherwise staunch Trump supporters and members of his MAGA movement. Hundreds of other comments included only images or memes, which were not analyzed, or did not directly address data centers or A.I.

The Times used an A.I. tool to help classify the sentiment of the posts and each user’s profile.

Some of the pushback on Truth Social has focused on the intrusion that data centers impose on rural areas, where more Republicans tend to live than Democrats. Data centers are massive installations that are increasingly being built in rural areas, particularly in the South. A few users suggested Mr. Trump build a data center at Mar-a-Lago, his Florida estate, to get a better taste of the disruption. One commenter criticized data centers and A.I. as tools of mass surveillance.

The explosive pushback is the latest sign that A.I. and data centers have become a thorny issue for Republicans this midterm season — a rare topic in the campaign that has united the majority of Americans in common concern.

A poll published on Tuesday by The New York Times and Siena University found that a majority of likely voters oppose building data centers, but that Republicans, while divided on the issue, were still more open to them than Democrats or independents. The poll found that 49 percent of Republicans supported such construction while 47 percent opposed it. Three quarters of Democrats and 60 percent of independents opposed them.

Polling from Pew Research Center last November also showed that concern over A.I. more generally has grown since 2021, rising to half of all Republicans in 2025, up from 45 percent in 2021.

“It really doesn’t play well to his base because a lot of those folks are probably worried about A.I. taking their jobs,” said Raymond La Raja, a professor of political science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, who has also conducted polling on the issue.

Mr. La Raja added that even if Mr. Trump’s base agreed with the president’s stance on A.I., that support may quickly erode. “If things start to unravel with A.I. and we start seeing major social disruptions, you’re going to see him do a quick reversal,” he said.

The growing concern over data centers has prompted some politicians, including many Republicans, to push back on their development in tight midterm races.

The issue has become a top concern in Pennsylvania’s governor race, where Josh Shapiro, the Democratic incumbent, and Stacy Garrity, his Republican challenger, have battled over who opposes data centers more. Mr. Shapiro signed an executive order seeking stricter guardrails for their development, while Ms. Garrity has vowed to pause such developments if elected.

A fresh wave of concern burst into public view last week when a researcher at Anthropic, an A.I. company, quit over fears that the technology was advancing at a dangerous pace.

Mr. Trump responded on Monday, posting on Truth Social that guardrails were not needed for A.I. because the United States was led by a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.” By midday, he posted that A.I. was “the Golden Goose” and should not be killed. Then, in the early afternoon, he posted that fears about A.I. “taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad” were nothing more than “a HOAX” — similar, he said, to two impeachment efforts against him and the federal investigation into his campaign’s interactions with Russia in 2016.

His comments drew immediate pushback.

Even some supporters who saw the logic of Mr. Trump’s support feared what would happen after he left office, giving other leaders control over A.I.’s future.

The pushback resembles what happened after Mr. Trump started a war with Iran this year and then posted about it online. Many users stormed the replies, disparaging his actions and expressing remorse about having once supported him as “the peace president.”

item.title: McCarthy Gets a Portrait Marking His Brief, Strange Speakership
item.description:
During the lowest moment of his long slog to become House speaker in 2023, Representative Kevin McCarthy sat in his office listening to the Republican standing in his way rattle off a long list of demands.

“Matt, it sounds like you want to be speaker,” Mr. McCarthy told Representative Matt Gaetz of Florida.

“You’ll get the portrait,” Mr. Gaetz fired back.

“I’ve got a lot of pictures of myself; I don’t need a portrait,” Mr. McCarthy said, using an expletive, before angrily tossing Mr. Gaetz out of his office.

But on Tuesday, Mr. McCarthy — who made history both as the man who took the most ballots to be elected speaker and the first speaker to be ousted from the post — got the official portrait marking his short and tumultuous tenure after all.

The gold-framed painting, an oil-on-linen by the artist Chas Fagan, was unveiled on Tuesday afternoon during an elaborate ceremony in Statuary Hall attended by Cabinet officials and members of Congress past and present.

Mr. McCarthy served as speaker for just 269 days, but his portrait will now hang in the Capitol in perpetuity. It is a testament to the brief, strange tenure of a Republican who served as a bridge between the establishment-led G.O.P. and the party it became after being fully subsumed by President Trump.

The portrait, which shows Mr. McCarthy standing by an open window with a slight smile on his face, captures his sunny personality and optimistic outlook, which he kept up even while proving himself to be a glutton for political punishment.

Mr. McCarthy, a mainstream Republican who was blamed for helping to rehabilitate Mr. Trump after the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection at the Capitol by flying to Mar-a-Lago and posing with him for a photograph, left Congress before Mr. Trump returned to power. (Mr. Gaetz left soon after.)

Mr. McCarthy’s tenure in leadership and the issues he was forced to deal with — a debt ceiling negotiation with President Joseph R. Biden Jr. and multiple spending fights that divided his own party — seemed like they belonged to another era as former colleagues gathered on Tuesday to honor him.

First elected to Congress in 2007, Mr. McCarthy, a proud Californian, was the party’s strongest fund-raiser in the House and spent two election cycles helping to build the Republican majority that ultimately rejected him as its leader.

“Everyone got to witness his legendary tolerance for pain,” former Representative Patrick McHenry, the North Carolina Republican who served as interim speaker after Mr. McCarthy’s ouster and his longtime confidant, said in his remarks. “Few people have sacrificed more for House Republicans over the past two decades than the man sitting before us today.”

An elegant program distributed to attendees memorialized that pain as a virtue in a brief biography: “In January 2023, Mr. McCarthy won the speakership after a historic 15 ballots,” it said.

Among his achievements, it listed securing “$2 trillion in deficit reduction, all while protecting the full faith and credit of the United States” — a rosy description for a debt ceiling deal that averted a federal default but reduced deficits by about half that amount. It also credited Mr. McCarthy for “keeping our government funded and making sure our troops were paid,” the bare minimum that is expected of Congress, but tasks that proved to be steep challenges while overseeing a tiny and fractious majority.

Despite Mr. McCarthy famously tripping over his words and often speaking in word salads, Mr. McHenry said that he demonstrated a “mastery” of politics, leverage and people.

Also in attendance at the portrait unveiling: John Ratcliffe, the C.I.A. director; Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, as well as his predecessor Kristi Noem; Senator Tim Scott, Republican of South Carolina; Representative Steny H. Hoyer, Democrat of Maryland; and the former White House budget director, Mick Mulvaney, among others.

The walls of the speaker’s lobby — a long, carpeted corridor outside the House chamber where members gather between votes — feature the portraits of more than 20 former speakers. Several more hang in the halls around the Capitol.

The tradition of hanging portraits dates to 1852, with the donation of a portrait of Henry Clay, who served as speaker three times, from the artist Giuseppe Fagnani. The House began mandating oil paintings of speakers in 1910.

Mr. McCarthy may have told Mr. Gaetz that he did not care about the portrait, but on Tuesday he choked up as he thanked his friends and former constituents for the honor.

“I loved every minute of every day I was able to serve,” he said.

item.title: Scrutiny of Jury May Complicate Future of Lindsay Clancy Case
item.description:
When several jurors from the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy spoke publicly last week about their deliberations, they probably did not imagine what would follow: Deep dives into their social media histories. Hateful memes depicting the women among them as crones. And excavation of two jurors’ past legal problems — none of which would have disqualified them from serving.

With a retrial of Ms. Clancy still possible, the intense scrutiny of the jurors whose deadlock led to a mistrial could complicate attempts to seat a new jury, from a pool of candidates who now have reason to fear a similar backlash.

The prosecutor in the case, Timothy J. Cruz, has not said if he intends to retry Ms. Clancy, 36, for the strangling deaths of her three children in January 2023. She has admitted to killing Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months. But according to the defense, she was experiencing postpartum psychosis at the time.

As Mr. Cruz weighs his next step, Ms. Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, could try to argue that the lone holdout juror would never have been seated if a past criminal accusation against him had been known.

The holdout — who voted for Ms. Clancy’s conviction while the other 11 jurors wanted to find her not guilty by reason of insanity — had been charged with misdemeanor domestic violence assault in 2021 after his wife at the time said he had grabbed her throat and thrown her against a dresser. That charge was later dismissed. Court records from the couple’s eventual divorce indicated that they had lived separately since the day of the arrest.

Then, last year, a teenage family member, who had called 911 during the 2021 incident, asked a judge for a restraining order against the man. The yearlong restraining order expired last month, during the trial.

Another juror identified the holdout in an interview with The Boston Globe, and The New York Times verified the holdout juror’s identity. Repeated efforts to reach the man, a 48-year-old resident of Plymouth County, Mass., were unsuccessful. Several of his relatives declined to comment on his background or his jury service.

Neither the restraining order nor the dropped misdemeanor assault charge would have disqualified the man from jury service under Massachusetts law, which bars only those with a pending felony charge or a felony conviction within seven years of their screening. Similarly, another Clancy juror — who was charged with misdemeanor assault more than 20 years ago, a charge that was also dismissed — was legally eligible to serve on the jury.

Unknown is whether the two jurors disclosed their past interactions with the law on the forms they filled out when they reported for jury duty. The Massachusetts form asks prospective jurors to “check all that apply” from a list that includes having ever been arrested, sued, served with a court order, charged with or convicted of a crime.

The form requires a signature from prospective jurors, acknowledging that “a willful misrepresentation or omission of a material fact on this form is a crime,” punishable by a fine.

In theory, lawyers on either side could have run background checks on prospective jurors, a review permitted until the jury is sworn in. But in reality, experts said, trial lawyers often lack the time and resources to independently scrutinize jury pools during the initial screening, known as voir dire, which tends to move quickly.

“They’re looking at the things that are immediately front and center, like race, youth, gender, occupation, and asking what they can glean there,” said Rosanna Cavallaro, a law professor at Suffolk University. Lawyers may challenge the other side’s choice of a juror for a range of reasons, and may also deploy a limited number of no-cause challenges.

She noted that questions on juror forms help guide lawyers in asking questions during jury selection that elicit candidates’ feelings about their past experiences, such as lingering animosity toward the police or the courts.

Defense lawyers often welcome jurors with past charges or convictions, experts said, because they may be more sympathetic toward defendants, or view prosecutors critically. The holdout juror in the Clancy case took the opposite stance, supporting the prosecution.

Even if a juror did fail to acknowledge being charged with or convicted of a crime , it wouldn’t necessarily be grounds for removal, Professor Cavallaro said. Such an omission could be accidental, and would likely be seen as less serious than “proactive” juror misconduct, she said, such as posting on social media about a trial while serving as a juror for it.

Because Ms. Clancy’s trial ended in a mistrial, effectively restarting the case, it is unclear whether, or how, the revelations about the jurors’ histories could be used by lawyers to affect what happens next. The same goes for the claim from other jurors that the holdout did not follow the judge’s instructions, or the law, in reaching his decision that Ms. Clancy should be held criminally responsible.

In the days after the mistrial was declared, every new bit of information about the jurors to emerge was seized on by many who had followed the trial closely.

Last week, one of the jurors in the majority revealed to Gayle King on CBS Mornings that the lone holdout was Black — and apparently the only Black person on the panel. That touched off a furor online from people who saw race as a pernicious factor in other jurors’ criticism of him. Conservative commentators, some of whom who had been portraying the holdout juror as a heroic white man, quickly pivoted to criticizing the optics of 11 white jurors trying to have a Black man removed.

Online sleuths also uncovered posts from a Facebook account that appears to belong to a juror who favored acquittal. They show her cheering on the acquittal of Karen Read, a defendant in another recent high-profile trial that, similar to the Clancy case, became a hotbed of conspiracy theories.

Jurors’ past conduct can have dramatic consequences. In another well-known Massachusetts case, a federal appeals court overturned the death penalty sentence of Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the Boston Marathon bomber, in 2020, after finding that the judge in the case did not sufficiently screen jurors for bias.

Two jurors, it was later discovered, had posted comments on social media about Mr. Tsarnaev before the trial and failed to disclose them. The forewoman referred to him as “that piece of garbage”; another juror called him “scum.” (The Supreme Court later reinstated the death sentence.)

Ten days after the judge declared a mistrial in the Clancy case, the intense scrutiny of jurors prompted unusual action on Monday. Judge William Sullivan indefinitely shielded the names of the 12 jurors and six alternates, citing “real and present risk” of harm fueled by “daily, divisive attention” to the case.He also impounded for 10 days the names of every potential juror who was called to court the week that jurors were chosen, in late July.

Judge Sullivan’s attempt to lock their identities away from public view underscored the toxic new reality faced by jurors in high-profile trials, in an age of rampant, polarizing online discourse.

Alec Ewald, a professor of political science at the University of Vermont who has studied jury eligibility, said that excluding broad categories of prospective jurors with specific backgrounds — such as past criminal charges against them — could undermine the goal of assembling a true “jury of one’s peers.”

But he added that in a case involving disturbing, unimaginable crimes, and sharp national division over what the outcome should be, it seemed natural that a mistrial, with its lack of resolution, would trigger frustration with the jury.

“There’s a need to make sense of these awful events, and then, with a mistrial, the jury gets in the way of that,” he said. “The ambiguity and complexity of having regular people make these decisions really comes home to us when the results are unsatisfying.”

Sheelagh McNeill and Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

item.title: Melania Trump Encourages Children to Build ‘the Next Great Robot’ With A.I.
item.description:
Melania Trump, the first lady, visited an elementary school in North Carolina on Tuesday, where she waded into the national debate over artificial intelligence and urged her audience of fourth through six graders to build “the next great robot.”

When a reporter asked about children using A.I. given growing concerns, Mrs. Trump seemed mostly to brush off the doomsday scenarios some industry leaders have been warning about — including mass unemployment, a new wave of biological weapons and autonomous warfare. President Trump had a day earlier dismissed such concerns in a torrent of social media posts, declaring them a “hoax.”

Mrs. Trump didn’t go that far.

“Of course, they need to be vigilant,” she said of the children of America. “But this is our future, and we need to guide them and teach them what, what is available. If not, they will stay behind, and we need to be the first in United States to lead.”

Before touring classrooms at Mountain View Elementary School, Mrs. Trump told the students: “I am especially excited to hear about your work with A.I.”

In her first classroom visit, the first lady walked around and talked to students about their projects. The children used balloons and a bottle to show how the organs inflate, then used A.I. to turn pictures of their model into a video simulation.

“Who’s on the right track?” she asked. “Are you figuring it out?”

Ms. Trump’s rare solo trip coincided with a roiling debate about the future of A.I. Over the weekend, Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, called for a global slowdown of artificial intelligence development in an extensive essay that was endorsed by several other industry leaders, including Elon Musk.

Mr. Trump spent Monday rebuffing them He maintained that the industry did not need guardrails, because it already had “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.”

Mrs. Trump has been a champion of A.I. during her husband’s second term. Last year, she warned that “the robots are here,” and said leaders “must manage A.I.’s growth responsibly.” And in March, she appeared at the White House alongside Figure 3, a humanoid, A.I.-powered robot, and said children may one day be taught by humanoid educators.

She did not show up to Mountain View Elementary School on Tuesday with a robot.

But she made it clear that she wanted to see more of them.

Mrs. Trump announced a partnership with Nvidia to bring more A.I. technology to the school district, including subscription licenses to a learning program for more than 1,000 students in the Ashe County School District, and low-power, agentic-ready A.I. computers for 100 students at Mountain View.

“Dream big and use these A.I. tools to build something never created before,” Mrs. Trump told the students. “Maybe one of you will create the next great robot. And if you do, make sure you bring it to the White House to show me.”

Mrs. Trump chose to visit Mountain View to return to the community that she toured with Mr. Trump last January after it had been hit hard by Hurricane Helene.

During her remarks to students who sat cross-legged in the gymnasium of the school, which was closed for more than one month and served as a recovery site for the community after the hurricane, Mrs. Trump linked the use of technology to the community’s resilience.

“Think about that remarkable journey: from floodwaters to the cutting edge of artificial intelligence,” she said.

Mrs. Trump was particularly animated as she sat between two little girls and their yellow robot during a demonstration of how students program robotic arms to complete tasks such as stacking blocks, and even eating, asking: “How did you start?” and “What is your next project?” before telling them both, “Beautiful job.”

During her nearly two hour visit, she gave out hugs, high-fived a young girl who told her she was in charge of her team and encouraged nearly every student she encountered to “Keep going.”

Jerry Graybeal, the principal at Mountain View Elementary, said that he understood the debate about A.I. and other technology, and the school was heeding warnings. But he said he was amazed at what the students had shown they could accomplish — the robotics that Mrs. Trump observed, he said, the students had received and assembled in one day.

“We’re limiting everything we do, but we understand the value, and that’s preparing kids for the future and the use of AI in the correct way,” he said.

Mostly, he was overcome that a school that only a year ago resembled a Walmart, stacked with basic necessities that the community could come shop for after the hurricane, was hosting the first lady at all.

“It’s unbelievable,” he said. “I mean, of all the schools in the country, we are probably the only one this year that receives that visit. And just to show our kids that it doesn’t matter where you’re from, what you have, what’s possible, you know?

item.title: Pentagon Inspector General Details U.S. Losses and Challenges in Iran War
item.description:
Some of the most detailed information about the Iran war has come not from the office of the defense secretary or the White House, but from a report released by the Defense Department’s inspector general.

The independent oversight agency offered glimpses into the U.S. military’s inventory shortfalls, and the damage from Iranian counterattacks to consulates and other diplomatic facilities in the region.

The document, which was issued on Monday, covered only the first four months of the war, from Feb. 28 to June 30. On Tuesday, the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office said in a separate report that war had cost the United States roughly $38 billion through Aug. 1.

Here are some key takeaways from the inspector general’s report.

The Pentagon and White House have said that their goal in Iran is to destroy its nuclear programs, attack drones, ballistic and cruise missiles, and its means of producing those weapons.

But the inspector general’s report noted that the Pentagon’s full mission statement for the Iran war “is classified.” That suggests that the military may have other goals that have not been made public.

The inspector general said that “it can be difficult to calculate the total ‘cost’” of the Iran war, given that the Pentagon has never had a separate appropriation from Congress to fund it.

Noting that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth did not request additional funds from Congress before launching combat operations, the report stated that funds for the war are coming from the department’s existing budget for training and maintenance of the force.

The costs to repair or replace U.S. military facilities damaged or destroyed by Iranian attacks — such as the Navy’s base in Manama, Bahrain — have not been calculated, as the Pentagon has indicated it may choose to close or not rebuild them.

On June 24, the report said, the White House submitted a $67 billion supplemental funding request for the war, of which $21 billion was slated for replacing munitions expended up to that point.

The inspector general also said that the State Department estimated that its embassies, consulates and other diplomatic facilities in the Middle East had suffered about $184 million in damage from Iranian strikes.

The U.S. diplomatic mission in Iraq was hit by “more than 600” Iranian attacks just in the first four months of the war, sustaining more than $157 million in damages.

The Pentagon’s top acquisition office told the inspector general’s office that the expenditure of munitions in the Iran war “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls.”

Military leaders have tried to speed up the production of munitions, the report noted, but added that “the defense industrial base requires ‘significant lead time’ to expand production capacities” for weapons.

Bottlenecks persist in the production of solid rocket motors that missiles rely on, as well as the supply of “high-grade explosives and propellants.”

The Congressional Budget Office report also found that the war had significantly depleted U.S. munitions. In response, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that “claims of U.S. munition shortages are false.”

The U.S. military force in the Middle East supporting the war has numbered roughly 50,000, even as units rotate on deployment.

According to the inspector general’s report, the war has seen “a dozen each” of fighter squadrons, destroyers and air defense batteries deployed as well as mobile launchers for artillery rockets and guided missiles like ATACMS and PrSM.

The war has also seen the deployment of four aircraft carrier strike groups thus far, and a “partial deployment” of the 82nd Airborne Division.

Iranian counterattacks damaged and destroyed “hundreds of buildings and structures” at U.S. military bases in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, the report said.

Additionally, dozens of U.S. military aircraft have been damaged or destroyed, including 30 Reaper drones, 12 KC-135 aerial refueling planes, four F-15 fighters and an A-10 attack jet.

The Defense Department has limited medical treatment facilities at every location where U.S. forces are deployed in the region, the report said, and has built more advanced facilities to provide surgical support in several countries.

For care beyond what those facilities can provide, the Pentagon has relied on hospitals in those host nations.

Medical evacuation helicopters in Iraq and Kuwait had to be relocated after Iranian strikes, the report said, adding that the “the nature of operations” during the war has meant most U.S. casualties have been transported by vehicles and ambulances to medical treatment facilities.

The U.S. has suffered 18 killed and 824 wounded in the war, according to a Pentagon casualty database.

The destruction of the Navy’s main logistics hub in Bahrain forced the Pentagon to look for additional supply ships that were outfitted to transfer fuel and supplies to warships at sea, the report said.

The Navy’s move to use the British-owned island Diego Garcia — roughly 2,200 miles from the Arabian Sea — as its new logistics center means that supply ships have to spend two to two and a half weeks to travel to the island, take on goods and fuel, and return to the Navy’s main operating areas outside the Persian Gulf, according to the report.

Of all the Pentagon’s “combatant commands,” which are responsible for military operations in different parts of the globe, U.S. European Command, based in Germany, has provided the most support to the Iran war, according to the report.

It transferred “munitions, equipment, aircraft and personnel, and requisitioned and distributed fuel, food, and medical supplies” to Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East.

Mr. Hegseth ordered Pacific Command, which is based in Oahu, Hawaii, to pursue and board suspected Iranian merchant ships in the Indian Ocean — expanding the mission far outside the Middle East.

Pacific Command was also ordered to give up six warships for the Iran war. They included the aircraft carrier strike group centered around the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln, which left San Diego on Nov. 21 and spent roughly nine months at sea without a port call for its crew to rest.

The ship is currently returning to its home port in Southern California.

item.title: Trump Plans Blitz of $138 Million and Counting to Save Midterm Republicans
item.description:
President Trump’s political operation has unleashed its vast financial resources to try to save the Republican Party’s control of Congress, reserving nearly $138 million over the past 10 days to help the party’s midterm candidates.

The planned spending linked to Mr. Trump’s $400 million super PAC has grown by the day, and is set to fuel a massive ad campaign supporting battleground Republican candidates beginning this month. Some Republicans for months have criticized Mr. Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., for not seriously engaging in the midterms despite its huge war chest.

But now a blitz of spending tied to the group has arrived.

A new super PAC that The New York Times previously reported was linked to MAGA Inc., No Going Back PAC Inc., has booked over $95 million worth of ads, according to data from AdImpact, a media tracking firm.

Another $27 million worth of ads is slated to come from another new super PAC called Safety and Affordability PAC Inc. The group is financially backed by MAGA Inc., according to two people with knowledge of the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to disclose a confidential arrangement. The group has not yet begun advertising.

The paperwork for No Going Back and Safety and Affordability was filed with the Federal Election Commission six minutes apart by the same treasurer.

So far, Safety and Affordability PAC has appeared to focus on helping House Republicans. It has booked ads in 15 races for the lower chamber. No Going Back PAC, by contrast, has booked two-thirds of its ad reservations on Senate races. And MAGA Inc. itself has booked another $9 million in ads — so far only in the Texas Senate race.

The three super PACs seem to have essentially carved up the midterm map; so far, their only overlapping advertising spending is in just two House races, New York’s 17th District and Michigan’s 4th District.

In addition to the ad reservations, the super PACs have also spent about $6.5 million on direct-mail efforts and about $80,000 on text messages, according to F.E.C. records. Together, the three groups are slated to spend about $138 million on ads, mail and texts to help Republican candidates in about 50 general-election races, spending the most on Senate contests in Michigan, Ohio and Alaska.

The House races with the most planned spending by the Trump operation are in New York’s 17th District, Florida’s 25th District and Michigan’s 4th District.

Details on the precise financial arrangement between MAGA Inc. and the two newer super PACs remain unknown, and could be revealed in future filings with the F.E.C.

The two newer super PACs appear to be so-called pop-up groups, appearing late in an election cycle and spending heavily before they are legally required to disclose their donors.

The two groups were formed in quick succession on Sept. 1 by Charles Gantt, a Republican political operative who specializes in campaign finance, according to F.E.C. disclosures. Both of the super PACs’ websites are nearly identical in design, down to the same boilerplate text that each group “makes independent expenditures in U.S. federal elections in support of candidates who share the values of the founders and funders” of each group.

Mr. Gantt did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The spending should quiet Republicans who harbored suspicion that Mr. Trump’s political group would hold close to its resources for his own political projects. The trio of Trump groups are, together, slated to be the biggest ad spenders in the November elections outside of the super PACs tied to congressional leadership, according to AdImpact data.

item.title: Black Bear Euthanized at Grand Teton National Park, Officials Say
item.description:
A black bear at Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming was euthanized on Friday after it began to show a “concerning pattern of behavior,” the authorities said on Tuesday.

The bear, who had been fed repeatedly by park visitors, had become an “unacceptable safety risk,” the National Park Service said in a news release. The bear was used to accepting people’s food, and that drew the animal closer to tourists near Delta Lake, the release said.

“We need to be clear — this bear was lethally removed because of poor decisions made by park visitors,” the park service said.

Grand Teton employees had received reports earlier this year that a black bear was approaching visitors near Delta Lake, a turquoise pool at the foot of soaring peaks. The number of recreationists hiking to the pristine waters has sharply increased, and the lake is one of the park’s most popular destinations, officials said in June.

But the park’s staff could not determine whether the bear was becoming conditioned to being fed by people or if the close encounters were an “isolated occurrence,” the park service said. “That changed last week,” it said in the release.

The bear recently approached visitors several times as people repeatedly offered food. The park’s employees found the bear “unusually difficult to haze away,” the release said. To address the safety risk, wildlife experts immobilized the bear by using darts and euthanized it in the park.

“A bear that gets a food reward can learn that approaching people pays off,” the park service said. “What may seem like a small decision in the moment can have serious consequences for the bear, other visitors and park staff.”

Right before autumn, black and grizzly bears are beginning hyperphagia, or when the animals devour as much food as possible to build fat reserves for the winter, park officials said last week.

The bears typically chew fruits — such as huckleberries, mountain ash and hawthorn berries — as well as white bark and pine nuts, officials said.

But the berry yield this year was “noticeably poor,” so the bears might roam widely for more food, officials said. Black and grizzly bears live all throughout the Grand Teton National Park, which straddles Wyoming and Montana.

“That means you may be more likely to encounter a bear on the trail,” officials said.

Visitors should never approach a bear or leave food out in the open. If a bear comes near while eating, store away the food and slowly retreat, officials added.

Food should be stored in a locked vehicle or a bear box, officials said.

“Help us keep bears wild by making the right choice every time,” the release said.

item.title: House Directs Trump to Halt War With Iran or Secure Congress’s Approval
item.description:
The House on Tuesday voted for a third time to direct President Trump to end the war in Iran or seek explicit authorization to continue it, delivering another bipartisan rebuke to his handling of the conflict as fighting in the region continues and American voters increasingly disapprove.

Seven Republicans joined Democrats in supporting the resolution, which does not carry the force of law but seeks to compel the administration to either halt the operation or win a vote of Congress approving it. But the action in the Republican-led chamber was the latest sign of frustration on Capitol Hill over the ongoing conflict and its domestic impacts, including high gas prices, weeks before midterm elections in which control of Congress is at stake.

Lawmakers voted 220 to 204 in favor of the resolution, which was offered by Representative Seth Moulton, Democrat of Massachusetts and a combat veteran, who said the war with Iran “has not only failed, but backfired.”

Since the conflict began on Feb. 28, Congress has collectively held 19 Iran war powers votes, six in the House and 13 in the Senate.

Mr. Moulton and his colleagues pointed to depleted munitions stockpiles, rising energy costs and a far lengthier war than the weekslong foray that Mr. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth promised when they began bombing Iran at the end of February.

Several of the Republicans who broke with the majority of their colleagues to vote in favor had done so on previous votes, including Representatives Tom Barrett of Michigan, Warren Davidson of Ohio, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Thomas Massie of Kentucky. They were joined by Representatives Nancy Mace of South Carolina and Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn, both of Iowa, who previously opposed efforts to restrict military operations against Iran.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Mr. Nunn, a combat veteran, said in a statement after the vote. He also noted that among the 18 U.S. service members who have been killed since the war began, two were from his home state. “Congress owes them, their families and every American in uniform clear objectives and constitutional oversight.”

It was the latest move by Democrats to highlight Republican backing for the war as polls show it is increasingly unpopular with the voters they need to maintain their majorities in Congress. A national poll conducted this month by The New York Times and Siena University found that the conflict, which has driven gas prices above $4 a gallon, is weighing down the president’s approval rating, with more than three-quarters of independent voters saying they disapproved of his handling of the war, along with nearly a quarter of those who supported Mr. Trump in 2024.

Democrats who backed the measure said the president had circumvented Congress in violation of the Constitution to unilaterally undertake an overseas war for which the administration has provided no clear direction, timetable or set of objectives.

“This Congress has not authorized a war with Iran, and yet this administration has kept our troops in harm’s way without a declaration of war, without an authorization from Congress and without any plan for how to win or end the war,” Representative Gregory W. Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee, said when the measure was debated on Monday evening on the House floor.

Though the vote was the fifth time that a bipartisan majority in one chamber of Congress has voted to direct Mr. Trump to end the war, the president continues to refuse to involve the legislative branch and shows no signs of winding down the military campaign.

The Times/Siena poll found that only 31 percent of likely voters approve of the war with Iran. Among Republicans, that figure is much higher, with 77 percent in favor. But among independent voters, a group that could play a critical role in the midterm elections, the numbers are even more lopsided, with only 21 percent of those polled approving of the war.

Antipathy has grown as the conflict continues to affect both the global economy and energy costs in the United States. The average cost of diesel fuel reached a record $6 per gallon last week, and rising energy prices are affecting air travel, farming and a number of sectors that have ripple effects for American consumers.

The direct costs of the war from Feb. 28 through Aug. 1 reached roughly $38 billion, the Congressional Budget Office reported on Tuesday, but the figure was limited because the Pentagon declined to provide details about how much had been spent.

The latest House rebuke of the war came as Republicans in the Senate were also growing more frustrated about the conflict.

Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican who has so far opposed efforts to rein in Mr. Trump on the war, said on Tuesday that he would now support such a measure. “It is time to be clear on the strategic objectives and start measuring results,” Mr. Tillis said. “And that’s not something that we’ve had since they started the conflict.”

Mr. Tillis initially backed the administration’s assertion that congressional approval was not necessary, maintaining that Mr. Trump was within his constitutional authority to direct the military for 60 to 90 days without congressional approval. That period passed in the spring, but Mr. Tillis still deferred to the president.

On Tuesday, he said that since the administration began characterizing the conflict as a war in mid-July, that started a two-month clock for Mr. Trump to secure authorization, which has now lapsed.

“It is important to start saying we deserve an update,” Mr. Tillis said. “Congress can be of assistance with this war effort if you inform us.”

item.title: Helicopter Crashes in Los Angeles County, Killing 3
item.description:
A helicopter crashed in Los Angeles County late Tuesday, killing three people, according to the Los Angeles Fire Department.

One of those killed was a passerby, according to Branden Silverman, a spokesman for the fire department, who spoke to reporters near the crash site in Chatsworth, a Los Angeles suburb. The number of people in the helicopter and their conditions were not clear, he said. He declined to confirm whether the aircraft was a news helicopter.

The fire department said in an alert shortly after that the death toll had increased to three people, and that the resulting fire damaged four vehicles and two shipping containers. It did not provide information about the other two people who were killed. One person was also taken to a hospital and their condition was unknown.

The helicopter crashed between two commercial buildings just before 7 p.m., according to an earlier alert from the fire department.

An NBC4 Los Angeles anchor said during a live broadcast that the station had lost contact with one of its helicopters but it “can’t confirm anything other than a television news helicopter has crashed.”

This is a developing story and will be updated.

item.title: Teachers Want Screen Time Limits in School, Too
item.description:
Fed-up parents who want less screen time in school may find allies in their children’s teachers.

About 73 percent of U.S. teachers strongly or somewhat support setting a maximum amount of time that students can spend on school-issued devices during the school day, according to a survey released Wednesday by Gallup, the Walton Family Foundation and the Joan Ganz Cooney Center, a research lab at Sesame Workshop.

And six in 10 teachers believe students should spend less time on laptops and tablets during school hours.

But teachers were less clear on how to do that, now that devices are used for everything from testing to textbooks.

About 54 percent of teachers said that at least part of their school’s curriculum could not be taught without devices. And in middle and high school, most teachers said it would be “very” or “somewhat difficult” to coordinate a daily time limit across multiple classes.

School districts across the country are facing a mounting backlash to the technology, led by parents. The nation’s two largest school districts, New York and Los Angeles, started this school year with new restrictions on student screen time and artificial intelligence.

The survey, which polled 2,100 teachers working in kindergarten through 12th grade in public schools in May, found that student device time — and the distractions that come with it — were less pervasive for younger students.

In elementary school, students spent an estimated 27 percent of their class time on devices for instruction or other permitted, noninstructional tasks, according to teachers. Relatively few elementary teachers reported that devices were a major or moderate distraction.

But in middle and high school, students spent nearly half of class time on devices for instruction or permitted, noninstructional tasks. Students also spent an additional 10 percent of class time on off-task, unapproved activities, according to the survey.

The extra, off-task time can quickly add up and “is a lot of what’s driving parents to push back on technology in the classroom,” said Medha Tare, senior director of research at the Joan Ganz Cooney Center, which is focused on digital media that can improve students’ lives and well-being.

Idle device time is in some cases replacing time students might have spent reading a book, doodling or chatting with friends, she said.

Four in 10 middle school teachers and five in 10 high school teachers reported that devices were a major to moderate distraction, with students often finding workarounds to school web blockers.

Still, teachers saw the benefits of technology, particularly for students who are learning English, students with disabilities or advanced students who need more challenging material.

Overall, teachers were split on whether technology is overall more helpful or harmful, with 52 percent saying student laptops and tablets in school cause “equal amounts of harm and good.” High school teachers were the most negative, with a third saying devices in school do “more harm than good.”

Even more than blanket time limits, teachers wanted more oversight over student devices and options to use technology more purposefully, the survey found.

Teachers who had “a lot of oversight” over student devices were the least likely to report student distraction and the most likely to say that technology helps students learn. About three in four teachers said that they could view student screens remotely, and about two in three said they could lock student screens remotely.

A vast majority of teachers supported stronger filtering for student devices, and many wanted clearer direction about the learning goals of various technologies.

More than 90 percent of teachers supported investing in more printed materials so teaching on computers was not their only option.
